articles.title_orig: Fostering rural sustainability in Europe and China
articles.title_zh: Fostering rural sustainability in Europe and China
articles.content_orig:
From cooperatives in Europe to agroforestry in China, the NEXRUR project is examining how community-led business models can strengthen rural resilience on both continents.
The EU-funded NEXRUR (opens in new window) project was launched in 2025 to help European and Chinese farmers and communities boost rural resilience. Now entering its second year – and having spent the first 12 months laying the foundations for its research on community-led sustainable business models – the NEXRUR consortium recently met in Uppsala, Sweden, to further develop its research agenda.

“The first phase was important to set up the conceptual and operational ground for pursuing NEXRUR’s research objectives in close collaboration with the case partners and relevant practitioners,” explains NEXRUR’s coordinating team at Leibniz Institute for Agricultural Engineering and Bioeconomy, Germany, in a press release (opens in new window) posted on the project website. “For instance, we did establish the so-called innovation network for mutual cross-case learning, and set up the stage for the National and European Stakeholder Panels that offer continuous input from the most relevant stakeholders surrounding the NEXRUR practice cases. Focusing on aligning our common research agenda at this meeting was important to ensure efficient, aligned and structured collaboration among our international consortium.”

Despite their diverse cultures, histories and economic realities, Europe’s and China’s rural areas share many challenges, ranging from climate change and biodiversity loss to ageing populations and depopulation. On both continents, rural communities look for ways to create new opportunities, producers strive to capture more of the value they create, and rural businesses aspire to combine economic viability with social and environmental responsibility. NEXRUR aims to identify novel solutions by combining complementary experiences in community-led development, cooperative models, technological innovation and climate resilience strategies.
The meeting in Uppsala marked an important step in advancing towards the next phase of research and implementation. Over a period of two days, researchers and practitioners held collaborative sessions at the campus of NEXRUR partner Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences. Discussions revolved around research questions and methodological approaches, data collection strategies and expected results, as well as the future development of the project’s research outputs. The meeting also offered the opportunity to coordinate subsequent stakeholder engagement and the selection of start-ups that will participate in the project’s activities.

A focal point of the discussions was the integral role that local communities play in rural business development. Underpinning this is the idea of community-ledness – the degree to which communities themselves initiate, shape, govern and benefit from such ventures. NEXRUR’s real-world cases (opens in new window) span a wide range of territories, value chains and organisation models across the two continents, from cooperatives, agroforestry and aquaculture to urban agriculture, local food production, circular economy solutions and agricultural technologies involving farmers, consumers, businesses and local authorities. By comparing these diverse experiences, the project aims to understand what helps rural business models succeed, what barriers they face, and how promising approaches can be adapted or replicated.

Following the meeting, NEXRUR (NEXT GENERATION SUSTAINABLE BUSINESS MODELS AND MONITORING FOR RURAL RESILIENCE AND INNOVATION) partners visited the Swedish island of Gotland to gain further insight into the realities of rural communities and businesses. As the project begins its second year, the focus will be on working more closely with its community cases and start-ups, collecting and analysing evidence, and gaining a better understanding of how community-led business models contribute to rural resilience in different contexts.

For more information, please see: NEXRUR project website (opens in new window)

articles.title_zh: China is among the U.S.’ leading espionage threats. Donald Trump doesn’t seem worried.
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .

SHENZHEN, China — President Trump has begun an extraordinary visit to Shenzhen, where he is set to join the leaders of Russia and China — two of Washington’s principal geopolitical rivals — for an unprecedented trilateral summit Thursday.
Chinese President Xi Jinping personally welcomed Trump on the tarmac upon his arrival, reciprocating a rare honor Trump extended to him during his September visit to Washington.
All three leaders attended a dinner alongside other regional heads of government on Wednesday night, participating in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, known as APEC.
The trilateral meeting will be the first of its kind by leaders of the United States, Russia and China, three nations with the world’s largest nuclear arsenals.
But while Trump has embraced a strategy of diplomatic engagement with historic foes, the three leaders enter the meeting with starkly different agendas.
Russian President Vladimir Putin hopes to secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine. Trump says he would like to discuss a nuclear arms control agreement and his war in Iran. And Xi aims to present China as a superpower on the international stage, capable of forging world peace.
Meeting with Putin before Trump arrived, Xi said that China’s relationship with Russia had remained as steadfast “as a rock through wind and rain.”
The two sides, he said, would pursue a “multipolar world” — a vision for a global balance of power that would see American influence weakened across Europe and Asia.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit.
Trump, for his part, has hedged on his expectations of the summit, signaling resolve against China ahead of his arrival here.
On Monday, the Trump administration tightened export controls on semiconductor chips essential to artificial intelligence development, closing loopholes aimed at curbing Chinese efforts to circumvent restrictions — a move that Trump acknowledged might be an “insult” to Xi before the meeting.
Chinese officials said Wednesday afternoon that Beijing reserved the right to retaliate.
“In essence, the United States is simultaneously trying to find limited avenues of cooperation with China while trying to clamp down on their access to critical parts of the AI supply chain, which doesn’t set up the conditions for productive dialogue,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Trump also met in Manila on Tuesday with fellow members of the Quad — India, Japan and Australia — in a show of resolve toward Beijing.
“Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Trump said in the Philippines.
“We continue to protect peace through strength,” he added.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO as US probes alleged chip exports to China - VOA
articles.title_zh: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO as US probes alleged chip exports to China - VOA
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's board of directors said on Monday that it has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO.
The action comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned amid a scandal over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China . China has denied it. Huang also had an extramarital affair with a subordinate at Nvidia, according to a New York Times report .
"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Board Chair Harvey C. Jones said in a statement on Monday.
"In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the company added.
Eleven days after his resignation, Huang said in a statement that he is "honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution." He also thanked the company's board, interim CEO Colette Kress, and Nvidia staffers and shareholders.
"I can't wait to get back to work," Huang added.
The decision to restore Huang to his position came as a major surprise. In a company earnings call last week, Jones said the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
Huang's affair with a woman believed to have links to China's Ministry of State Security has put a spotlight on Nvidia's business in the People's Republic, with lawmakers questioning whether the company's AI chips were winding up in China in violation of U.S. export rules.
Huang last week underlined his eagerness to return to the chip company he co-founded in 1993, saying that if the "board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."
Numerous business leaders and thousands of Nvidia employees had signed a petition urging the chipmaker to rehire Huang. President Trump had also suggested that he would support the leader's return to Nvidia. "I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said last week.
In a social media post on Monday, Mr. Trump cheered Nvidia's move.
"The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," Mr. Trump said on Truth Social. "The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security."
Mr. Trump also told CNBC that he had spoken directly to Nvidia's board about reinstating Huang.
Dan Ives, a tech analyst with Yorkville Ives, told CBS News that the board "had no choice" but to bring Huang back as CEO, saying that the executive's shock resignation earlier this month was becoming an "economic and global markets issue."
Nvidia makes advanced chips and other components that help power AI, which is driving economic growth in the U.S. and until recently had fueled record stock market gains.
"Nvidia is the linchpin to the global economy," Ives said.
Gil Luria, lead tech analyst at investment adviser D.A. Davidson, attributed Nividia board's U-turn to White House pressure to reinstate Huang.
"Because there is so much concern about the health of the overall economy and ability for the U.S. to continue to grow the AI investment cycle, which was accentuated by stock market declines last week, the White House wanted to put him back in his seat to move the economy forward," Luria told CBS News.
Nvidia's stock soared more than 30% on news of Huang's reinstatement. The news also buoyed other stocks, with the Nasdaq Composite Index erasing all of its losses in early trading after a steep sell-off on Friday.
Other Wall Street analysts who follow Nvidia expressed surprise at the company's sudden turnaround, but said the executive's return bolsters the company and the broader AI sector.
"Jensen was a singular CEO who built Nvidia into an AI juggernaut and maintained an extremely flat corporate structure, making him difficult to replace," Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge told investors in a report.
Under Huang, Nvidia has emerged as a pillar in the growing AI industry, not only through its technology prowess but also for its role in financing the purchase of advanced chips and striking other deals to stoke demand for its products.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq post best day since April 2025 as Nvidia stock soars 31% on Jensen Huang's return
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq post best day since April 2025 as Nvidia stock soars 31% on Jensen Huang's return
articles.content_orig:
Stocks soared on Monday after Nvidia announced it would reinstate Jensen Huang as president and CEO, erasing losses from a major sell-off on Friday that plunged the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory.
The Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.2% in midday trading, regaining ground after the technology-heavy index fell 1,261 points, or 5.3%, on Nov. 20, its second-worst day of 2026. The S&P 500 climbed 4.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 2.8%.
Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scandal over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. On Monday, the board said it believes Huang is the "right person to lead Nvidia" and that it has "every confidence" in him as he resumes his leadership role at the company. Huang's reinstatement is "effective immediately," the board said.
" The company reported fantastic numbers last week, but the uncertainty of their leadership was like a huge overhang," eToro investment analyst Bret Kenwell told CBS News.
"Now that uncertainty suddenly is not only removed, but it's replaced with the very familiar leadership of Jensen," he added.
Nvidia shares surged more than 30% on Monday after the opening bell, quickly adding $1 trillion to its market value. Shares of CoreWeave, a cloud computing company and Nvidia customer, shot up 25%. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index, which tracks 30 of the largest companies involved in the design, distribution, manufacture and sale of chips, rose 14%.
"I believe the White House leaned hard on the board, and the message is crystal clear. America needs Jensen Huang leading Nvidia and, therefore, the wider AI industry," Nigel Green, CEO of investment advisory firm deVere Group, said in an email. "His return hands him more control than ever. He's got the backing of the board, the U.S. president and the market, and that's a phenomenal platform to take Nvidia to another level."
Despite Monday's market exuberance, some Wall Street analysts said investors remain on edge amid concerns that the artificial intelligence sector is unraveling.
"Stocks in the U.S. are staging a large rebound rally so far this morning, although, just to put things into context, the S&P futures aren't even reclaiming their loss from Friday, much less the entire week," Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli said in a note to investors on Monday before Nvidia announced it was reinstating Huang.
"Sentiment remains pretty bleak — most people are looking at this [Monday] uptick as nothing more than technical in nature, a partial reversal of extremely oversold conditions," he added.
Financial markets tumbled Friday as concerns swelled about a possible slowdown in data center construction across the U.S. and tightening restrictions on chip exports, both of which could hurt corporate profits.
The losses were led by microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom, which shed 13.3% and 12.2%, respectively. Both were recovering Monday, with AMD up 6.8% in midday trading and Broadcom gaining 1.2%.
Anthropic, which made its public market debut on Thursday, slid 2.5%.
Kenwell said financial markets still face headwinds, including a more hawkish Fed, high inflation and investor uncertainty over the AI trade. However, corporate profits remain strong, he said, citing Nvidia's robust earnings last week and bullish financial markets.
"That's not a today story," Kenwell said. "That was true a week ago, true a month ago, and it'll be true at the start of next month."

articles.title_orig: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock climbs more than 31% as board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.title_zh: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock climbs more than 31% as board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO , effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries.
The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk."
President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard."
Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.
Shares of Nvidia closed up 31% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6.
"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process."
Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said.
Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations.
Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."
He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."
"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote.
Several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk , CEO of SpaceX , Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected."
Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
For weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Nvidia's board formed an independent committee and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation into Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. The board said Monday that "the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion" and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it."
"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia's board chair, Harvey Jones, said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."
Even with Huang back at the helm, Nvidia is facing increased scrutiny over its chip sales in Southeast Asia and China.
Lawmakers have been preparing for investigations into how Huang's affair with the alleged spy may have damaged U.S. AI dominance, influenced his positions on export controls, and impacted his close relationships with Trump and his Cabinet. Huang has been one of the loudest voices opposing strict export controls on advanced chips.
"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., said in a statement Monday.
Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, is scheduled to appear before the panels on Dec. 2. Those dates were set before Huang's return, and John Fisher, who represents Huang, did not comment on whether there are any changes in his plans to testify.
Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Monday that Huang will publicly testify on Dec. 3 as the sole witness during a hearing titled, "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls."
"Americans deserve answers about what NVIDIA and the Trump administration knew, when they knew it, and whether sufficient steps were taken to prevent sensitive technology from falling into the wrong hands," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., a member of the Banking Committee, wrote in a post on X on Monday.

articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of AI tech giant Nvidia effective immediately following a scandal involving an alleged spy, the company's board of directors announced Thursday.
The decision came amid an investigation into Huang's affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. President Trump said this week the FBI is investigating romantic and business ties between Huang and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The two aren't related.
Nvidia's board had been preparing to oust Huang , two sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News on Wednesday night, plans that were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
Huang's departure also follows a New York Times report Wednesday that five employees at Nvidia came forward alleging Huang was romantically involved with a subordinate, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare.
The Times also reported Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were caught on video being affectionate at a conference in March, according to two Nvidia employees. The Times has not seen the video and CBS News has not verified the report.
After Huang's resignation was announced Thursday, the Reuters news agency reported that Huang also had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter. The agency only identified the employee as a woman.
The company's interim CEO will be Colette Kress, who is currently Nvidia's chief financial officer and will continue in that role.
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Harvey Jones, who was announced as the company's first board chair, said in a statement.
Kress has been Nvidia's CFO since she joined the company in 2013. She previously worked in finance roles at tech companies like Cisco and Microsoft for nearly 25 years.
Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993. It became one of the most valuable companies in the world by designing the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.
Nvidia's stock plunged as news emerged of the company's turmoil, potentially erasing almost $500 billion in value. In Thursday's trading, the stock price closed down 4.3% at $166.19.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an executive at Megaspeed International , a Singapore-based data center company whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Megaspeed grew with the help of access to Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips. According to U.S. investigators, Alice Huang was able to gain access to 240,000 chips that were banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
In Washington, top Democrats on Capitol Hill have expressed concerns over whether Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang may have compromised U.S. national security.
Following Jensen Huang's resignation, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said his departure doesn't absolve him or the company from the scandal.
"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren said in a statement.
Before Huang resigned, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News the departure could help China in the competition between Beijing and the U.S.
"With him out as CEO, China could significantly narrow the gap versus the U.S.," Ives said. He added: "The problem now is that there's no replacement for Jensen. It's a black eye moment for him, for Nvidia, and actually the U.S. tech industry. I'd say it's dark day for, you know, U.S. technology."
Following Thursday morning's announcement, Mr. Trump said on his Truth Social platform that there was "only one man" who could replace Huang: former Apple CEO Tim Cook .
Mr. Trump had a close relationship with Huang, who has attended AI-focused White House events and traveled with Mr. Trump to China. Late last year, Mr. Trump granted Nvidia the right to sell advanced H200 chips to "approved customers" in China, with the U.S. government getting a 25% cut — a major coup for Huang, who has long sought to sell more technology to the Chinese market. The deal did not cover Nvidia's even more advanced Blackwell and Rubin systems.
In a radio interview Thursday, Mr. Trump brought up that he gave Huang a National Medal of Science earlier this year. "What a horrible thing that is," he said of the situation involving Huang, adding, "That's so sad to see that happen."
The president also said in an interview: "What a horrible thing that is
In a statement accompanying her appointment as interim CEO, Kress said that the company's focus will be on "serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders."
"NVIDIA's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said.
The board said it will be conducting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates.
Jennifer  Jacobs , Jo Ling  Kent , Aimee  Picchi and Isabel  Vincent contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Moscow accuses Estonia of hostile actions on 'verge of triggering open war'
articles.title_zh: Moscow accuses Estonia of hostile actions on 'verge of triggering open war'
articles.content_orig:
Russia has accused Estonia of carrying out numerous “hostile actions” and threatened “open war” against the neighbouring Baltic state.
Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday accused Tallinn of a ⁠⁠range of hostile actions, asserting that the NATO and European Union member state is “on ⁠⁠the verge of triggering open war”.
The outburst comes after Estonia announced the planned closure of its border with Russia, and a Ukrainian attack on a Russian ship in the Baltic Sea.
The ministry set out its accusations in a statement after ⁠⁠summoning Estonia’s charge d’affaires in Moscow, Marek Uhtegi, to issue a formal protest over Tallinn’s decision to close the border.
“The Estonian diplomat was once again told that such provocative and extremely dangerous actions are on the verge of triggering open war with Russia,” it said, adding that Estonia is displaying “Russophobic” tendencies.
Among a list of additional accusations, the ministry said Estonia had “tacitly allow[ed] its airspace to be used by Ukrainian drones for attacks on northwestern Russia”. Tallinn was swift to deny the claim.
It also accused Estonia of trying to obstruct the movement of Russian cargo ships in the Baltic Sea, banning the transit of Russian and Belarusian grain, seeking a ban on the Russian language and threatening to close the Russian Orthodox Church.
“The Russian side reserves the right to take comprehensive political and diplomatic measures aimed at protecting Russia’s national interests and the legitimate rights of its citizens,” the ministry said.
Estonia is host to a sizeable ethnic Russian population, which Moscow has often claimed is subject to discrimination.
Russia’s incursions into eastern Ukraine in 2014 were based on claims of suppression of Russian speakers’ rights in the region.
Earlier this month, Estonia said it would close border crossings with Russia from December 1 for at least six months, having accused the Kremlin’s security services of staging an attempted arson attack on an Estonian defence company.
This marked a sharp escalation in tensions between Estonia and Russia, which Tallinn – Kyiv’s ally – sees as part of a broader campaign of hostile activity linked to Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
Russia has denied any involvement in the attack. Closing the border, the ministry said, “will inevitably backfire – not only on Tallinn itself but also on its allies within the EU and NATO”.
In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Estonia did not respond to all of the allegations but denied that it allows its territory to be used for Ukrainian military operations.
“While we generally do not comment on or engage with Russian propaganda narratives, in this case we can reiterate that Estonia has never allowed, and will never allow, its territory to be used for military operations by another country,” it said.
“Other countries in our region have also made this position clear,” it added.
Russia has long accused Estonia and other NATO states in the Baltic region of allowing Ukrainian drones to use their airspace. Ukrainian drones have frequently entered NATO airspace, but Kyiv says this is a result of Russian signal jamming.
NATO countries have repeatedly denied intentionally allowing drones to use their airspace, and blamed Russia for the incursions.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, speaking in Berlin, said the alliance was monitoring the situation in Estonia, along with an incursion last week by Russian missiles into Poland, adding that NATO had options available to respond.
“We see situations in Poland and Estonia, etc ,” Rutte said. “When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary.”

articles.title_orig: Anthropic options post solid debut, trailing SpaceX record
articles.title_zh: Anthropic options post solid debut, trailing SpaceX record
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Just two days after its public debut, the stock market's newest AI giant, Anthropic ( ANT ), looks to be missing out on Monday's major tech rally.
The stock of the Claude model maker fell 1.4% on Monday, trading below $88 as of 3:00 p.m. ET after whipsawing earlier in the day. Meanwhile, Nvidia ( NVDA ) and other AI-linked stocks, including CoreWeave ( CRWV ), soared amid the broader tech rebound that followed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.
The move comes after Anthropic's stock sank 9% on Friday following a 17% gain on its IPO day last Thursday. At Monday's current price, the stock is up about 5% from its $83 IPO price.
Read more: What investors should know about buying into Anthropic stock
The choppy performance might reflect ordinary post IPO profit-taking and broader skepticism about Anthropic's valuation. Needham analysts said in a Sunday note that the most common concern they hear from investors is whether the company can sustain its enormous revenue growth next year. The company's fully diluted IPO valuation of about $1.5 trillion is roughly 40 times trailing sales.
The stock also has a potential supply overhang. As much as 315 million shares held by insiders, roughly one-third of the stock the company issued in its IPO, became eligible for sale almost immediately, according to Anthropic's IPO paperwork.
Needham added that given Anthropic's staggered schedule for permitting insider share sales could bring more shares to market in the first six months.
Another key question hanging over the company is how credit markets will absorb the AI firm's massive spending needs. Anthropic has committed to spending about $900 billion on its computing and infrastructure needs for the next two decades , including $70 billion due over the next 12 months.
The AI boom's ravenous capital needs have flooded the bond market this year, becoming a looming concern for investors.
Investors expect the major rating agencies to assign a high-yield, or junk, rating to the company's debt, according to a Wall Street Journal report . No rating has yet been announced.
Anthropic's credit rating is key for the wider AI ecosystem. Getting the higher investment-grade rating would help offer some relief to chip makers, including Nvidia and Broadcom ( AVGO ), that have guaranteed billions of dollars worth of microchips to customers that lease compute power to major model makers like Anthropic and rival OpenAI. ( OPAI.PVT )
The high-yield bond market also comes with constraints, including smaller capacity and higher borrowing rates, for the newly public giant.

articles.title_orig: Xi pressed Trump on Taiwan at meeting in China, urged U.S. to halt arms sale
articles.title_zh: Xi pressed Trump on Taiwan at meeting in China, urged U.S. to halt arms sale
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Gets Hero’s Welcome Upon Return To Nvidia HQ, Video Shows
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Gets Hero’s Welcome Upon Return To Nvidia HQ, Video Shows
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO , effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries.
The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk."
President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard."
Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.
Shares of Nvidia surged 33% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6.
"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process."
Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said.
Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations.
Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."
He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."
"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote.
Several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk , CEO of SpaceX , Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected."
Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
For weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Nvidia's board formed an independent committee and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation into Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. The board said Monday that "the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion" and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it."
"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia's board chair, Harvey Jones, said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."
Even with Huang back at the helm, Nvidia is facing increased scrutiny over its chip sales in Southeast Asia and China.
Lawmakers have been preparing for investigations into how Huang's affair with the alleged spy may have damaged U.S. AI dominance, influenced his positions on export controls, and impacted his close relationships with Trump and his Cabinet. Huang has been one of the loudest voices opposing strict export controls on advanced chips.
"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., said in a statement Monday.
Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, is scheduled to appear before the panels on Dec. 2. Those dates were set before Huang's return, and John Fisher, who represents Huang, did not comment on whether there are any changes in his plans to testify.
Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Monday that Huang will publicly testify on Dec. 3 as the sole witness during a hearing titled, "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls."
"Americans deserve answers about what NVIDIA and the Trump administration knew, when they knew it, and whether sufficient steps were taken to prevent sensitive technology from falling into the wrong hands," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., a member of the Banking Committee, wrote in a post on X on Monday.

articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang may be back but the China hawks probably haven't given up
articles.content_orig:
Charles Gasparino is out with an interesting report. He argues that the Nvidia saga isn't over and for reasons that could rattle the equity bulls.
The drama is no surprise but this is a concern:
Now it's not clear that "stuff that is coming out" means news we already know about or conjecture but it's a reminder that there are powerful forces that don't like how Nvidia has behaved and don't want to see Huang succeed. Now maybe it's China hawks in a power play and they've now had their wings clipped or maybe the people fighting against open source AI really want to take Huang down.
So now we just have to wait for the next round of leaks. No one likes to hear about accounting leaks and the vendor finance is a real problem.
Shares are up 30% today but they've flatlined from the open. When people hear about accounting issues, they're inclined to take some off the table.

articles.title_zh: Exclusive / Commerce to add Megaspeed to trade blacklist
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration plans to add the company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, Megaspeed, to a trade blacklist designed to prevent it from obtaining US-made semiconductors, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The Singapore-based company will be added to the Commerce Departmentâs entity list on Monday, the sources said.
The addition means that no US company can sell certain technologies, including semiconductors, to Megaspeed or its foreign affiliates without obtaining a license from the US government. The news comes the same day the Nvidia board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO, after President Donald Trump implored them to do so. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scrutiny over his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under pressure to place Megaspeed on the departmentâs entity list from others inside the administration, tensions that became public after news broke of Huangâs relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who was an executive at Megaspeed. The Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed violated US export controls by shipping Nvidia chips to China.
Earlier this month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his agency along with the Pentagon, the State Department, and the US Trade Representative had backed putting Megaspeed on the entity list âfor monthsâ but that âCommerce holds the pen.â Bipartisan lawmakers have pressed Lutnick to put Megaspeed on the entity list and explain his decisions around Nvidia, Megaspeed, and chip export controls.

articles.title_zh: Poland to get NATO early-warning aircraft after Russian missiles hit country
articles.content_orig:
NATO will deploy an AWACS early-warning system aircraft to Poland as part of its response to ⁠three missiles landing in the country on the military alliance’s eastern flank, a Polish deputy defense minister said on Monday.
Three Russian Kh-101 missiles ⁠landed in Poland ​on ⁠Friday, prosecutors said, adding to fears that Russia’s war in Ukraine could spill ⁠into NATO territory.
“An AWACS early-warning aircraft ​will ⁠be made available to Poland,” ‌ Pawel Zalewski told reporters after a NATO meeting in Brussels. “This is a very ‌good system that gives us ‌even deeper... operational awareness which allows us to respond better to this kind of threat.”
With their distinctive ⁠nine-meter-wide radar domes, NATO’s 14 Airborne Warning and Control System aircraft have served as the alliance’s eyes in the sky since 1982.
Based at Geilenkirchen air base in Germany, the fleet has played an important role ‌in surveillance missions along NATO’s eastern ​flank since Russia launched its ‌full-scale invasion of Ukraine in ⁠2022.
In a conflict, they can ⁠provide a common radar picture for allied fighters, ships ‌and control ​centers, while directing NATO combat ‌jets to their ​targets.

articles.title_orig: States sue Musk companies over flood of sexualized images made with AI chatbot Grok
articles.title_zh: States sue Musk companies over flood of sexualized images made with AI chatbot Grok
articles.content_orig:
On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.
SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).
Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked . Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first , Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today.
Without intervention, kids in Virginia and Oregon risk a lifetime of distress, as Grok images will likely be impossible to remove online.
“Once created and shared,” Grok-generated CSAM and NCII “can never be fully erased, and it becomes a permanent record of the child’s abuse that may resurface for the rest of the child’s life,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones’ complaint said. “Virginia has a profound interest in protecting its children from this harm.”
Millions of residents were allegedly harmed, as the attorneys general seek to protect every Grok or X user in their state. Many Grok victims will likely suffer from chronic anxiety, depression, and PTSD, as well as reputational harm, as some viewers may not realize the images are AI-generated, the states alleged. Further—due to Grok’s integration with the social media platform X—users as young as 13 may have been exposed to the AI content and possibly re-traumatized if they, too, are victims of sexual abuse, the states alleged.
“xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield said in a press release.
States alleged that xAI could have conducted rigorous red-teaming to block outputs before the new feature launched. But instead, the X Safety team responsible for Grok red-teaming was reduced to two or three team members, states alleged.
Overall, rather than use industry-standard safeguards, Musk’s firms allegedly put profits over women’s and children’s safety, states alleged, while complaining that SpaceXSI won’t even publicly identify “the officers responsible for safety governance.”
“Industry standard requires not only building guardrails but also vigilantly monitoring whether they hold,” states alleged. SpaceXSI is doing neither effectively, states alleged.
Asked for comment, SpaceXSI shared an X Safety post on X, which repeated claims that the company has a “zero-tolerance” policy for “any forms of child sexual exploitation.” X Safety said that the company “acted promptly to tighten” Grok protections, which are supposedly “designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people.” That statement also claimed that X Safety continually tests and adjusts protections when bad actors find ways to avoid filters, while relying on “sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt” to catch harmful outputs “before an image is generated and check every output after.” Although the statement did not mention whether xAI sues users who break Grok rules to generate CSAM and NCII, it emphasized that xAI reports harmful content generated to police.
“When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement,” X Safety said. “Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors.”
However, state attorneys general alleged that reports from independent researchers and news outlets this year have shown that Grok is still generating NCII and CSAM. They noted that the chatbot “even advises users how to circumvent its own limited moderation measures to generate those images.” In some cases, a Virginia state probe found that Grok complied “with a user request to draft a prompt designed to avoid moderation.” So, even when filters work, the chatbot helps determined users immediately get around them, states alleged.
Nothing xAI did put a dent in the harmful outputs, least of all putting the feature behind a paywall , states alleged, which only ensured maximum profits. A troubled New York City Council speaker, Julie Menin, confronted SpaceX this October with proof that attempts to digitally undress her own photo still worked for free Grok users, states alleged.
Concluding its probe, Virginia found that moderation remains “inconsistent and ineffective,” with Grok sometimes carrying out prompts “that it later blocked.”
In its complaint, Virginia alleged that Grok protections “were weak, ineffective, sparsely enforced, and easily circumvented.” Oregon agreed that rather than act to protect users, SpaceX entities repeatedly made statements “with the intent to deceive consumers” that Grok was safe. Most egregiously to state attorneys general, in January, Elon Musk denied any harm to real people, claiming that Grok is only “supposed [to] allow upper body nudity of imaginary adult humans (not real ones) and only generated nudity of fake people (not real ones).”
“Contrary to Musk’s representation,” Grok “makes the same sexualizing edits to photographs of real, identifiable people,” states warned. “Defendants intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM, NCII, and non-consensual sexualized images,” they alleged, and other “contemporaneous statements by Musk make clear that Grok’s ability to create sexualized material was part of xAI’s business strategy.”
It’s also troubling to states that the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) reported to Congress that more than 90 percent of the Grok-generated CSAM that xAI submitted to its CyberTipline was considered a “dead end.”
As NCMEC explained, xAI initially refused to provide NCMEC and police with “basic user information, including location information, that law enforcement needs to act.” To fix the problem, NCMEC had to set up a meeting with xAI and get the reports resubmitted. This, states alleged, confirmed that “the information existed and that xAI had not provided it.” The concerning omission allegedly slowed down police response, just as the average number of Grok CSAM reports jumped by 88 percent from December 2025 to January 2026, then increased by another 66 percent from January to June 2026.
“X users were subjected to the risk that any person, at any time, could use their likeness to create CSAM, NCII, or other non-consensual sexualized images,” states alleged.
Lawmakers have asked state courts for an injunction blocking SpaceX entities from violating consumer protection laws by allegedly operating Grok without industry standard safeguards. If they win, they want SpaceX to pay thousands in civil penalties per violation, as well as disgorge any ill-gotten gains from marketing the chatbot as safe to users.
“Most people who use social media do not want to contribute to the harm caused to victims of CSAM, NCII, and other non-consensual sexualized images by being exposed to those images online,” states alleged.
Although Oregon’s complaint only vaguely estimates the number of users Grok attracted with Musk’s allegedly deceitful marketing strategy as at least “hundreds of thousands,” Virginia’s complaint included more detailed estimates. articles.title_orig: Mamdani to Cap E-Bike Rides at $3.65 for Citi Bike Members Starting Next Year
articles.title_zh: Mamdani to Cap E-Bike Rides at $3.65 for Citi Bike Members Starting Next Year
articles.content_orig:
Lyft will cap the Citi Bike member cost of any sub-45-minute e-bike trip at $3.65 starting on Jan. 19, Mayor Mamdani said on Monday, and the bike-share provider has also agreed to freeze member rates through the middle of 2029.
The Citi Bike-loving mayor’s announcement — first reported in the New York Times —comes ahead of a City Council hearing on Citi Bike fees scheduled for Dec. 2. All four bills on the meeting’s agenda would offer discount rides or cap rider fees. Council Speaker Julie Menin is scheduled to appear at the mayor’s Citi Bike announcement on Monday morning.
Lyft made $24 million off the bike-share system last year, according to publicly posted Citi Bike financial reports. Annual membership, meanwhile, has skyrocketed from $95 in 2013 to $239 today. Citi Bike’s only existing e-bike ride price cap is $5.40 for sub-45-minute trips into or out of Manhattan; a 45-minute e-bike ride not going into or out of Manhattan currently costs $12.15. Transportation Alternatives’ “Citi Bike Riders Union” campaign has called on the city to cap all e-bike rides at $3.
The company’s contract to run the city’s bike-share program expires on May 26, 2029, though no competitor could likely come close to meeting the capacity demands of the current Citi Bike system. That gives Lyft significant leverage in negotiations with the city.
Editor’s note: This story initially misreported that the new price cap will apply to e-bike trips into our out of Manhattan; it will apply to all e-bike trips.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia board shows "lack of backbone" in re-hiring Jensen Huang, governance experts say
articles.title_zh: Nvidia board shows "lack of backbone" in re-hiring Jensen Huang, governance experts say
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia’s intense boardroom drama, in which Jensen Huang was ousted and brought back in the span of less than two weeks, would not have been possible without questionable decisions by Nvidia’s directors.
Now, the board faces intense scrutiny over its role in a corporate soap opera with enormous consequences.
While Wall Street loves the shocking return of Huang at the helm of Nvidia, corporate governance experts are horrified by what they view as malpractice by the company’s board: With no chair prior to Huang’s ouster, no succession plan and the loosest of leashes on its CEO, the board had set itself up to fail.
Huang said he built the company so that he alone could run it – and the stock acted that way, losing $1.5 trillion in market value since the scandal erupted on Nov. 8. An outpouring of support for Huang from investors and partners followed, and a shareholder revolt seemed imminent.
The board, consisting of many long-tenured Huang supporters, announced its decision to reinstate Huang on Monday, after the same board unanimously accepted his resignation. And directors are bringing Huang back before the completion of a board-ordered investigation that was supposed to get to the bottom of allegations over whether Huang has been the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
President Donald Trump on Monday told CNBC he called the board and helped orchestrate Huang’s return. That put the board in a no-win scenario: Stand pat and risk getting ousted. Give in and appear weak and ineffective. (Nvidia declined to comment.)
Of course, it didn’t have to be this way. A strong board – one that provides vigorous oversight of the CEO and requires successors to be groomed – could have avoided this mess turning into a debacle.
“The board should resign. Every one of them,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management. “This is a complete failure of corporate governance.”
Huang stands accused of some serious violations of corporate policy. He acknowledged an affair after reports of a relationship with a major customer, and he was reportedly in a relationship with an employee.
Although the board on Monday said US government officials assured them rehiring Huang posed no national security risk, the investigation continues.
The seriousness of the allegations make Huang’s return all the more shocking from a corporate governance standpoint.
“The standard to apply is: Would we fire a middle manager for this behavior?” said Nell Minow, chair of corporate governance advisory firm ValueEdge Advisors. Potential espionage aside, Huang’s affairs would be grounds for dismissal, Minow argued.
Minow said she would favor the board resigning except that she fears Huang would just bring in people who are “even more compliant.”
But the board appears to have been backed into a corner.
The Nvidia scandal contributed to a market meltdown so severe that some suggested the AI bubble was popping before our eyes.
Huang was the He-Man CEO of AI, the industry’s de facto central banker and widely viewed as a visionary pioneer who transformed graphics processors into the lifeblood of AI computing. And he is buddies with the president of the United States.
Trump on Monday was effusive with praise for Huang, telling CNBC he personally called Huang and the board to help arrange his comeback.
“With pressure from the president and his administration, the board may have felt it had no choice, but this is not a board that has ever shown that it understands its obligations to shareholders or to the law,” Minow said.
The board failed by placing Huang above corporate governance, said Bill George, former CEO of Medtronic.
“The board does not appear to be in control,” said George, now an executive fellow at Harvard Business School.
The board didn’t have to let it get to this point.
For example, it could have opted to put Huang on leave pending the results of the investigation, which could have insulated it from outside pressure – even from the commander in chief.
But the problems started earlier. Without a succession plan, Huang effectively held the board hostage, said Sonnenfeld, the Yale professor.
Most well-run companies with functional boards have an emergency plan in place, in case the CEO is hit by a bus, suddenly resigns or needs to be disciplined. They also typically review potential replacement CEO candidates as part of their due diligence. There’s no evidence Nvidia had done any of that.
That, in part, gave Huang an aura of invincibility .
“Our company was built so that I know how to run it,” Huang told Bloomberg in 2023. “So, for as long as I’m running it, that’s all that matters.”
Nvidia has a deeply talented bench. So allowing a company to rely on a singular figure – who alone could account for trillions of dollars of company value – represents a complete failure of the board, Sonnenfeld argued.
Still, the board’s flip-flop may not be nefarious.
Ultimately, the board is tasked with deciding whether it can trust Huang and whether his ongoing presence at Nvidia is in the best interest of the company and its stockholders, noted Brittany Rogers, partner in the corporate governance practice at O’Melveny & Myers.
“There is no single ‘right’ answer here,” she said, calling the decision complex and difficult.
Although it may be easy to assign bad motives to the decision to rehire Huang, the board may also have been presented with new facts that changed its mind – even from a week earlier.
“I would apply the presumptions of the business judgment rule and assume that the directors acted on an informed basis, in good faith, and in the honest belief that each decision served Nvidia’s best interests,” said Lawrence Cunningham, director of the University of Delaware’s Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance.

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian naval drones strike a new Russian warship in Libya, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian naval drones strike a new Russian warship in Libya, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Anchored up in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.
The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi , co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes , has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.
Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.
The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.
And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".
Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.
Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.
If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?
As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.
On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders , just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.
This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.
It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders are becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.
But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much – but not all – of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.
Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.
In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.
The three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.
There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.
Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.
Hybrid warfare isn't new but it is on the rise.
It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.
This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.
There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

articles.title_orig: Amazon’s China-made adult bed rails recalled after 89-year-old woman dies of suffocation
articles.title_zh: Amazon’s China-made adult bed rails recalled after 89-year-old woman dies of suffocation
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of adult bed rails from China that were sold in the US have been recalled after an 89-year-old woman died of suffocation when she was trapped between the product and her mattress.
About 2,114 adult bed rails sold on Amazon by Guangzhou Yupin Technology Co. – a Chinese company doing business as Xentrawave – are included in the recall, according to the US Consumer Product Safety Commission.
All batches of Xentrawave’s model XT016 and batch number 20251212 of model XT026 are included in the recall for failing to meet mandatory safety requirements, because customers can be pinned between the rail and the side of the mattress – posing a risk of death by asphyxiation.
The XT106 model adult bed rail also doesn’t meet structural stability requirements and its push pins and push pin holes are incorrectly sized, posing a risk of laceration, the agency said.
The CPSC said it has received one report of a death related to the Xentrawave recall, involving the 89-year-old woman who died from asphyxiation.
Customers can find the model numbers XT016 or XT026 on the front of the product’s outer packaging and the first page of the instruction manual.
For the XT026 model, consumers can locate the batch number on the product label attached to the back of the bed rail’s gray fabric pouch and in the instruction manual.
Consumers should immediately stop use of the recalled bed rails and contact Xentrawave for a full refund.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
They will be asked to cut the foam padding on the bed rail handles, disassemble the product and email a photo of the destroyed bed rail to xentrawavedirect@163.com or submit it online at https://xentrawahelp.com/xentrawave-bed-rail-safety-recall/ .
The recalled XT016 bed rails were sold on Amazon from May 2025 through March 2026 and the XT026 model was sold from March 2026 through August 2026. The bed rails cost between $37 and $40.
The bed rails were manufactured by China-based Guangzhou Nanyu Medical Technology Co.
