articles.title_orig: Drone Attack Hits Colombian City as Unmanned Explosives Transform Conflict
articles.title_zh: Drone Attack Hits Colombian City as Unmanned Explosives Transform Conflict
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Earlier this month, drones flew over a military base in Santa Rosa del Sur, in Colombia’s Bolívar department, dropping explosives that killed three soldiers when detonated.
Just days before that in October, the Colombian military said a vessel assigned to Riverine Marine Battalion No. 42 was attacked in the Guapi River in a similar fashion, killing one Marine and injuring four others.
In September, a civilian radar in the Valle del Cauca region was damaged after what appeared to be an explosive-laden drone reportedly collided with it.
And a new attack occurred just this Saturday evening: the headquarters of a battalion in La Jagua de Ibirico, César department, were attacked with drones and explosives. One soldier died and at least 12 were wounded.
The incidents, analysts say, are the latest examples of militant groups operating drones in ways that mirror battlefield uses — leaving local governments to race to catch up with the technology needed to defend against them. And Colombia appears to be ground zero for what could emerged as a new wave of conflict against rebels and narco groups in South and Central America.
The explosive-carrying drones are “inexpensive, easy to acquire and useful for monitoring security forces and protecting illicit operations,” Rebecca Bill Chavez, former US deputy assistant secretary for defense for Western Hemisphere Affairs, told Breaking Defense.
Use of small drones by militant and drug-trafficking groups isn’t new, but Chavez, the president of the Inter American Dialogue, said a growing problem is that the groups “have gone from using drones to monitor troop movements to launching coordinated attacks with multiple drones,” including unmanned systems using fiber-optic guidance systems.
Expanding manufacturing capacity is critical to producing missiles, radars, and launch systems.
Colombia has emerged as the flash point since August, when a new government led by President Abelardo de la Espriella promised a “mano dura” — or strong hand — approach to countering cartel and other armed groups. The Colombian armed forces have carried out several major operations, including air strikes, against historic rebel groups like the ELN and FARC, as well as drug cartels like the Clan del Golfo, and other non-state criminal networks. (Each of the named groups have been declared a terrorist organization by the US State Department.)
In response, during just the first 100 days of de la Espriella’s term, Colombia has suffered at least 93 attacks that involved drones, according to country’s news agency Caracol Radio . Of the 26 Army personnel killed during these 100 days, “at least 11” were killed due to drone-dropped explosives. (Colombian insurgents generally do not take responsibility for drone attacks, with the government usually assigning blame.)
On Nov. 8 , the Ministry of Defense announced the seizure of a weapons cache, property of the Clan del Golfo, which included one drone and 35 grenades “conditioned to be dropped by this [uncrewed] aircraft,” suggesting that local insurgent groups are still investing in these weapons.
“There is no conventional drone warfare in Colombia,” a Colombian former army colonel told Breaking Defense on the condition of anonymity. “Rather, there are sporadic attacks against units in frontline areas which have no c-UAS [counter-unmanned aerial systems] protection.”
The surge in drone threats is likely to lead to greater investment in counter-drone systems.
The previous president, Gustavo Petro, announced Bogotá would create an “ anti-drone shield ” that would include fixed, mobile and man-portable counter-drone systems. But Colombia’s new defense minister, Jorge Eduardo Mora, said the effort hadn’t amounted to much by the time the new administration came in.
The Colombian armed forces do operate some counter-UAS systems. The Defense Ministry released photos of soldiers with jamming rifles on Nov. 8, stating that troops in the Chocó department had neutralized a drone to prevent “grenades from being dropped on soldiers.”
However, more systems are needed. The retired colonel explained to Breaking Defense that the armed forces require “air defense systems specifically for drone threats, both mobile and fixed.” Chavez agreed, saying “investing in counter-drone defenses is essential to protect soldiers, police, and civilians.”
One potential remedy, according to Henry Ziemer of the Americas Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, would be for Colombia to join the US-run drone and counter-drone marketplace , as Argentina, Mexico and Panama have reportedly done. In August, the US military sent out the first “tranche” of invitations to “selected international partners” with a second tranche to follow.
But relations between Washington and Bogotá may have become more complicated this month after The New York Times reported that de la Espriella had rebuffed an American offer of joint counter-drug operations — though de la Espriella denied the report . On Friday, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wrapped up a Central and South American tour, praising the closeness of US and Colombian militaries.
Still, getting help with counter-drone capabilities from the US or elsewhere and training up Colombian soldiers is only “part of the answer,” Chavez said.
“Without stronger intelligence and investigative capabilities, governments will keep responding to attacks without stopping the criminal organizations behind them,” she said.
“Who is supplying and modifying these drones? Who is training the operators?” she asked. “The goal should be to dismantle those networks, not just shoot down drones once they’re airborne.”
The retired Colombian colonel, a Lancero, said he agreed. The Ministry of Defense and other agencies “need to strengthen intelligence operations to locate where the narco-insurgents’ drone bases are,” he said.
And it’s not just Colombia. So far, drones carrying lethal explosives have also been used in attacks in Brazil and Mexico . Ziemer is pessimistic about the future.
“As knowledge of drone tactics proliferates faster than governments deploy countermeasures, it seems likely we will begin to see them crop up in more countries in the region.”

articles.title_orig: Stocks making the biggest moves Monday: Boeing, Nvidia, CoreWeave, Newmont & more
articles.title_zh: Stocks making the biggest moves Monday: Boeing, Nvidia, CoreWeave, Newmont & more
articles.content_orig:
The major indexes closed significantly higher on Monday.
The major stock indexes rebounded sharply on Monday as Nvidia shares closed up more than 31% after the company announced the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 1,147 points, or 3.0%, while the S & P 500 jumped 4.7%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq soared 6.5%.
Shares of Nvidia surged, recovering nearly all of the losses suffered since Nov. 12, the day Nvidia announced Huang's resignation .
Each of the three major indexes fell into correction territory last week, meaning they dropped at least 10% from a recent high.
The drop in shares last week owed to scrutiny centered on the artificial intelligence industry amid volatile trading in AI giant Anthropic's newly listed stock and uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.
The gains on Monday recovered much of those broad market losses.
The surge in tech shares, meanwhile, extended beyond Nvidia. Shares of Dell closed up 20%, while chip company Micron climbed 15%. SanDisk, a memory hardware firm, saw its stock price jump 10%.
CoreWeave, a cloud-computing company that focuses on AI, rose 22%.
Despite strong performance for AI companies, Anthropic shares ticked down more than 1%.
Nvidia reinstated Huang as president and CEO, the company announced before trading on Monday, less than two weeks after Huang resigned amid reports of an alleged affair with a suspected Chinese asset.
Huang will also hold a seat on the company's board, Nvidia said.
The company's board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA," Nvidia said in a statement.
"In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk," the company added.

articles.title_zh: Danish top court’s ‘ghetto law’ ruling supports hardline immigration policy
articles.content_orig:
Denmark's Supreme Court on Monday ruled in favor of a housing association that terminated 91 leases in order to prevent the label "hard ghetto" being applied to their housing complex. The decision align's with Copenhagen's hardline approach to immigration .
The court on Monday upheld Denmark 's 2018 "ghetto law," which allows for the relocation of "non-Western" residents from minority-heavy neighborhoods in order to foster integration . The Danish court ruling diverges from a top EU court decision last year that found application of the law could amount to discrimination.
The Danish laws requires social housing estates to rebuild, renovate and adjust their social mix if these become minority heavy, stipulating that 60% of apartments be rented to "Westerners" at market value by 2030.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Denmark's pioneering role in spearheading tougher immigration rules has made it a model for some in the EU . Denmark was also one of five countries that last week announced its intent to set up an asylum seeker deportation hub in Rwanda.
Danish Housing Minister Jacob Mark welcomed Monday's decision, saying it "strengthens security, social cohesion and integration."
The court's decision upheld a 2022 lower court ruling against seven tenants who fought their evictions in Nojsomhed, Helsingor, just north of Copenhagen.
In Monday's ruling, the law was found to be non-discriminatory when it comes to the eviction of "immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries" as it is not broadly based on ethnicity. The EU ruling focused on this particular aspect, saying the law would be discriminatory if criteria were race based, while ultimately allowing national courts to have the last say in the matter.
"The Supreme Court notes that applying the criterion of the law involves dividing people into two groups [immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries, and all other persons]. Both groups include a very large majority of different ethnic origins, and there will simultaneously be persons with the same ethnic origin in both groups," read the Danish court's ruling.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Tenants' associations estimate that 11,000 people across Denmark will have to be relocated to comply with the law.
The housing association in question issued a written statement saying that it was aware that the evictions would impact those affected, adding that it undertook measures to insure that residents found new homes.
According to Statistics Denmark's definition, "non-Western" countries include every country other than the 27 member states of the European Union, as well as Andorra, Australia, Britain, Canada, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the United States and the Vatican.

articles.title_orig: Over 700,000 Russian Soldiers Have Died in Ukraine, Analysis Indicates
articles.title_zh: Over 700,000 Russian Soldiers Have Died in Ukraine, Analysis Indicates
articles.content_orig:
Meduza, Mediazona, and more than a dozen other journalistic teams will present the results of an independent analysis of Russian mortality data tonight, after 5 p.m. CET . The data came from the hacker groups Cyber Partisans of Belarus and SilentCrow, who obtained it after hacking Rosstat’s database.
We and colleagues from other independent outlets spent more than two weeks examining the leak, verifying its authenticity and searching the records Rosstat received from the EGR ZAGS for data on losses among Russian troops since the start of the full-scale war.
All the journalists who worked on this project concluded that the database is largely authentic. Final loss estimates may vary between outlets, depending on how each includes or excludes certain categories of the dead. Not every death can be definitively linked to combat operations, even using the leak’s detailed cause-of-death data. As a result, estimates of Russian military losses vary depending on how that link is interpreted and on the nuances of counting. We will explain in detail why we are confident our own count is accurate.
The EGR ZAGS data in the leak include only registered deaths. For military personnel, the delay between death and registration can run six months or longer, and the share of these late registrations has been growing. As a result, a significant share of the dead are missing even from Rosstat’s internal data, especially over the past year and a half.
Estimating the true number of Russian military losses, accounting for these late registrations, therefore requires research that draws not only on the EGR ZAGS leak but also on many other independently obtained data sets and statistical modeling. Meduza will publish an estimate of these “invisible” deaths alongside its analysis of the Rosstat leak.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected] .
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter .

In case you missed it somehow, there's been quite the fuss made about a certain video game released last week for consoles only — although the PC version of GTA 6 might be nearer than you think, especially given the most recent development in this arena.
I'm talking about the unofficial (and obviously illegal) porting of the console game to the PC, of course, but the interesting wrinkle here is that some very fast progress on this front could mean the actual PC port from Rockstar arrives much more swiftly, to cut off any competition at the pass, as it were.
What has really stirred things up here is that, as Eurogamer reports , there's been a development whereby Cyberleek — a hacking group (most likely a team, anyway, but it could be an individual) — has released what's apparently a dev build (from this month) of the Xbox version of GTA 6 .
Cyberleek had threatened that they would release the full game in the past, and this appears to be the realization of this threat, with various sources confirming that the game files and assets are real (and total 209GB). For example, TweakTown highlights that cybersecurity group VX Underground believes the leak is genuine, and theorizes that Cyberleek obtained the GTA 6 build by compromising a Rockstar Games employee.
This happened at the tail end of last week, but today is of particular interest because there was one thing missing from the leaked game build — the central EXE (executable) file that runs GTA 6 , and Cyberleek has said they will release that final piece of the puzzle at some point on November 23.
If that happens today, and a fully working Xbox build is effectively out there, it could mean big things for a PC port. The availability of an unencrypted full version might usher in a working PC build sooner than everyone was expecting — and the separate development of various emulators (for running console games on PC) has already raised expectations on that front.
Indeed, according to Cyberleek, the release of the EXE will mean that: "This community will have it [GTA 6] emulated inside a week, running far past 30fps. [Cyberleek] told you not to preorder for a reason. This is one of the reasons."
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Cyberleek added that if "the Xbox build cannot be made to work and support holds", they will work to get a PS5 build as a "fallback, most likely never required".
Whatever the case, it seems Cyberleek is serious about their threats, and the releasing of the EXE today. It would have been released before now, incidentally, if their crypto coin had hit a market cap of $15 million — the promise was that it would be leaked as soon as that happened, or on November 23 failing that.
So, are we going to see GTA 6 fully up and running on the PC soon in an unofficial manner? Well, there's a lot of ground that hasn't been covered yet, and for starters, the release of that EXE file still needs to happen. Most folks seem to think it will, though, and there's no real reason to doubt that given what's happened to date and Cyberleek's track record ( they previously leaked footage of them playing the game before GTA 6 was released, back in August).
Even so, if we assume that the unencrypted executable is leaked later today, and the full Xbox version is then available, there's still some way to go before the various community projects on the boil out there produce an unofficial playable version of GTA 6 on the PC.
The key word there being playable . Whatever initial fudged version of GTA 6 on the PC arrives will surely be in rough shape, and likely crash-prone with perhaps all manner of glitches.
It's also worth noting that we obviously don't condone piracy at TechRadar, and there are obvious dangers associated with any unofficial PC build. There are bound to be malware packages masquerading as versions of GTA 6 trying to trick PC gamers into downloading them — and indeed that's happening already, as scammers who are nothing to do with Cyberleek try to exploit the situation around this possible PC version . Such activity will likely only increase if the EXE is released today as promised.
Whereas there's a lot that's up in the air around this affair, and the broader drive to emulate console games on PC, what's quite clear is that all of this is doing PC gamers a major indirect favor. Because the pace of progress with emulation and getting GTA 6 unofficially running on the PC means Rockstar may bring the release date of the official PC port forward in a major way. If the rumors are to be believed, that port could be due early in 2027 , and this executable leak — if it happens as stated — is going to put even more urgency into bringing forward the official release timeframe.
As one Redditor put it : "If this [Cyberleek leak] is real, we're actually getting GTA 6 on PC before Rockstar even announces it. Maybe this finally forces them to move the official release up."

"Yelling fire in a crowded theater moment is here and the bears will take center stage with this narrative and ultimately with Jensen out at Nvidia, market fears globally, and the Blue Tidal Wave in DC going after Big Tech this will be bumpy road over the coming months," Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said in an X post.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street analysts cheer Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia — but they still have concerns
articles.title_zh: Wall Street analysts cheer Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia — but they still have concerns
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Bernstein analysts were quick to upgrade Nvidia ( NVDA ) on Monday after the board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO of the AI chipmaker, though Wall Street sees ongoing investigations as a lingering overhang on the company.
The stock surged as much as 32% following Huang's reinstatement. President Trump said he spoke to the board and "convinced" them to reinstate Huang.
Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon and his team, which had downgraded the stock to a Neutral-equivalent Market Perform rating just 11 days ago, rerated the stock as Outperform as soon as the board announced Huang's return.
"As we remain positive on AI buildout fundamentals, and with Jensen back in the seat, we upgrade today back to [Outperform] (as his exit was the primary reason for the downgrade)," Rasgon wrote.
The analyst maintained a $200 price target, highlighting questions that will likely leave some overhang in place, including ongoing investigations which may limit NVDA's multiple for now.
"While we are happy to have Jensen back, the on-again-off-again response from the board is, frankly, clown-like," the analysts added, questioning what this says about how the board goes about making other decisions.
Yorkville's Dan Ives, which has maintained a Buy rating on the stock, said on Monday that the firm believes Nvidia stock should be valued at $300 with Jensen Huang back. However, the analysts kept $225 as the price target for the stock, saying they're looking for a resolution of the board's investigation.
The path to closing the price gap "runs through the committee's conclusion, a clean read on the export probe, and a 4Q print delivered by a CEO whose tenure is no longer a topic on the earnings call," Ives wrote.
KeyBank analyst John Vinh stated that while Jensen Huang's reinstatement is a "significantly positive development," the firm retains a Sector Weight, or Neutral, rating and awaits further clarification on the board's ongoing investigation and the SEC accounting inquiry before revisiting its rating,
Stifel analyst Ruben Roy, meanwhile, reiterated a Buy rating and maintained a $205 price target, noting that while Huang's return removes key-person risk, the ongoing investigations remain a potential overhang on the shares.
Several other analysts echoed the sentiment that a major overhang has been cleared, even as governance questions remain. In other words,
"In our view, the reinstatement removes the key overhang created by the CEO transition," Citi analyst Atif Malik wrote, issuing a Buy rating and raising the firm's price target to $240.
Malik noted that while Huang's reinstatement "restores continuity across NVDA's product roadmap," uncertainty remains around the scrutiny into Huang's relationships. "That said, we would view clean resolutions of these concerns as a further catalyst," Malik added.
Others pointed toward Nvidia shares responding to an overcorrection in selling.
Analyst Tristan Gerra noted that while Baird retained its Neutral rating, "near-term the stock has over-corrected and we expect a rerating towards our price target driven by the return of Mr. Huang as CEO."
"I am still a buyer of Nvidia today," Antoine Chkaiban, New Street Research analyst, said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I think there's still plenty of upside with the stock. It's still very cheap. You know we have Nvidia generating 25 bucks of earnings in 2028. So the stock is still trading below ten times that [on a PE ratio]. And I think there's plenty of upside."
Correction: A previous version of this article misstated Stifel's price target. We regret the error.

articles.title_orig: China’s Naval Developments Set For The Spotlight At Zhuhai Airshow
articles.title_zh: China’s Naval Developments Set For The Spotlight At Zhuhai Airshow
articles.content_orig:
China’s People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) says it’s preparing a major presence at the upcoming 16th China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition in Zhuhai, with warships , carrier-based aircraft , advanced weapons systems, and uncrewed platforms set to feature prominently. The expanded naval component will include a new maritime equipment exhibition area at Gaolan Port, located just on the other side of the bay, marking the first time the PLAN has established such a dedicated display at the event.
Zhuhai has become one of the most important events on the international defence and aerospace calendar, serving as China’s principal public showcase for its rapidly developing aviation and military industries. First held in 1996, the biennial China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, commonly known as Airshow China, provides an unusual opportunity to see some of the country’s most advanced military hardware, including aircraft and systems that are rarely shown in such detail elsewhere. While the event also serves as a major platform for China’s aerospace industry to promote its products to potential international customers , it has increasingly become an important venue for revealing new military capabilities and offering glimpses of programs that are otherwise difficult to assess.
Previous editions have produced some particularly significant developments. The 2016 show saw the J-20 stealth fighter make its first public flying appearance , while the 2018 edition provided an unusually revealing look at the aircraft, including a demonstration of its internal weapons bays, loaded with air-to-air missiles . The 2022 exhibition featured the J-20 on static display for the first time at Zhuhai, alongside the Y-20 heavy transport aircraft, Z-20 helicopter, and YY-20 aerial refueling tanker, which made its first flying demonstration at the event. More recently, the 2024 exhibition was particularly notable for the public debut of the J-35A stealth fighter and the appearance of the catapult-capable J-15T carrier-based fighter.
This year’s exhibition, scheduled to take place from December 7 to 13, will showcase, among others, a broad range of the PLAN’s capabilities, with a particularly notable emphasis on the rapid evolution of its carrier aviation capabilities, something we have addressed in detail in the past . Among the most noteworthy aircraft expected to feature are the J-15T carrier-based fighter, the operational J-35 stealth fighter, the KJ-600 carrier-based airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft, several naval variants of the Z-20 helicopter, and, perhaps most significantly, the new JL-15 carrier-capable trainer, a development of the land-based JL-10 .
While we have seen the J-15T at Zhuhai before, the aircraft will be of particular interest if it is shown with the indigenous WS-10H2 engine. Such a configuration would offer a closer look at the latest evolution of China’s carrier-based Flanker derivative and its ongoing transition toward a more domestically supported carrier aviation ecosystem.
The appearance of the J-35 would be another major highlight. The aircraft represents a significant step in the PLAN’s carrier aviation ambitions, bringing a fifth-generation stealth fighter capability into the carrier air wing. Its presence would provide another opportunity to examine the progress of China’s next-generation naval fighter program. Back in 2014, Zhuhai saw the public debut of the FC-31 fighter demonstrator. At the time, it was still a land-based concept, and export was the main talking point, although there was already speculation about a naval variant, today’s J-35.
Meanwhile, the KJ-600 is arguably one of the most important developments in the PLAN’s carrier aviation ecosystem. The twin-engine turboprop aircraft is designed to provide airborne early warning and battle management capabilities, something that would transform the situational awareness and coordination available to China’s carrier strike groups.
Several variants of the Z-20 family are also expected to feature, reflecting the growing importance of helicopters in carrier operations, including airborne anti-submarine warfare, utility, and other maritime support missions. You can read more about the Z-20 family and other Chinese rotary-wing developments in this previous TWZ deep-dive on the topic .
Perhaps the most intriguing aircraft on the list, however, is the JL-15.
The JL-15 is derived from the Hongdu JL-10, also exported as the L-15 Falcon, a twin-engine advanced jet trainer and lead-in fighter trainer. The navalized development was initially reported to be designated JL-10J, but is now confirmed as being the JL-15. A tailhook-equipped mockup was spotted alongside the aircraft carrier Fujian in 2024. However, its operational status remains unclear, and China is known to have encountered difficulties with its earlier JL-9G naval trainer, whose tailhook was reportedly deleted following structural problems.
Regarding the rumoured JL-10J carrier-capable jet trainer, another hint was spotted next to the carrier Fujian: It appears to be an unfinished JL-10J mockup stored on the dockside . So question is: Two tails as shown in the latest CG or just one like the regular JL-10? pic.twitter.com/BM8W8MRGWK
Its appearance would provide a particularly interesting indication of how China is thinking about training its next generation of carrier-based pilots. A carrier-capable development of the JL-10 would be an important addition to the emerging carrier aviation ecosystem, bridging the gap between conventional jet training and the demanding requirements of operating from an aircraft carrier.
The JL-15 also makes an interesting comparison with the U.S. Navy’s somewhat stuttering efforts to introduce a new training jet for its carrier pilots.
The U.S. Navy’s Undergraduate Jet Training System (UJTS) program is intended to replace its aging fleet of T-45 Goshawk trainers, but the acquisition effort has encountered considerable difficulties. Earlier this month, we described how Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) withdrew its proposed clean-sheet Freedom Jet from the competition, citing concerns over the Navy’s insistence on firm-fixed-price production commitments before the aircraft’s design had sufficiently matured. This leaves the Beechcraft M-346N , based on Leonardo’s established M-346 Master , as the only publicly known remaining contender . The program has also experienced schedule slippage, with the initial contract award now expected in the fourth quarter of Fiscal Year 2027.
Perhaps more significant is the difference in the two services’ approaches to carrier aviation training. The U.S. Navy has removed the requirement for its next-generation jet trainer to be capable of operating from an actual aircraft carrier, including carrier qualification and simulated carrier touch-and-goes at land-based facilities. Instead, it increasingly relies on advanced simulation, virtualized training, and assisted carrier landing technologies to prepare pilots for the demands of carrier operations. The JL-15, by contrast, is intended to support carrier-based pilot training. A dedicated carrier-capable trainer could offer China a more direct pathway for preparing pilots for operations aboard its increasingly sophisticated — and expanding — carrier fleet.
Taken together, the PLAN aircraft being lined up for Zhuhai this year illustrate the increasingly sophisticated and integrated nature of China’s carrier aviation ambitions . As well as the aircraft carriers and their embarked aircraft, these ambitions also require other surface and subsurface vessels to operate effectively.
Uncrewed systems will form another important part of the display. The exhibition will include aerial drones, uncrewed underwater vehicles, and other autonomous platforms, reflecting the PLAN’s growing interest in the potential of uncrewed warfare. Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona said to expect "a stronger hearing than normal" when lawmakers have a chance to grill now-reinstated Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang next week.
"What I want to know is the exact tick-tock of how this all occurred," Gallego said, listing questions such as when Huang learned about suspicions of his paramour's involvement with Chinese intelligence, and whether he purposely helped her company evade a ban on semiconductor exports, as well as President Trump's involvement.
"I think it does bring sharper questions into focus," he added.
Gallego spoke to Yahoo Finance on Monday shortly after the Senate Banking Committee, where Gallego sits as a member, confirmed that Jensen's testimony will go forward on Dec. 3 .
Gallego's comments underscore the battle Huang will face in Washington in the months ahead, despite having Trump's backing .
Many lawmakers, even in Trump's own party, are not fully on board with Huang's reinstatement. Hard questions in the hearing a week from Thursday are likely to come from both sides of the aisle.
Another member of the panel, Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts of Nebraska, posted on X Monday, listing issues dogging Huang, such as his reported multiple affairs and lack of "candor" with his own board of directors.
"His behavior does not support reinstatement," Ricketts wrote.
Gallego's comments were part of a flurry from Democrats who quickly promised aggressive oversight when they take power in January.
"Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives," Chuck Schumer, the likely Senate majority leader, wrote on X .
"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate's banking panel and in line to take over in 2027, said in a statement in which she called Huang's reinstatement "a reckless decision."
Gallego — who is mentioned as a possible 2028 presidential candidate — said he also wants to hear from members of Nvidia's board of directors, as well as officials at the Commerce Department who ran the semiconductor export control program, whom he called "the executioners of this."
He said he is keenly interested in whether the president or members of his team, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, profited from Nvidia's gyrating stock or previous loopholes in semiconductor exports.
Gallego and his colleagues will also likely have a second opportunity to probe these issues with Lutnick, who has agreed to testify publicly , potentially on Dec. 10.
Gallego said he expects that Lutnick will appear, noting that if he tried to avoid testifying in 2026, he would face a Congress in 2027 with Democrats in control.
In that case, Gallego said, "I think he's going to find himself in a worse situation."
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
articles.title_zh: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
articles.content_orig:
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.
Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.
Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".
Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".
And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.
Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?
The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.
Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.
This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.
Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.
He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.
Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.
"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.
The wider political backdrop was still more revealing.
The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.
And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.
The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.
Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.
Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.
Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action.
So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them?
The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels.
Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received.
"This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared.
Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU."
Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies.
The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance.
So is it possible for a majority of countries to outvote those blocking progress?
The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, has acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible. Others want countries prepared to move faster to make their own agreements outside the formal talks.
But there is a reason the UN climate process depends on consensus. International climate co-operation is largely voluntary.
Voting might produce more ambitious agreements on paper, but would it persuade the governments that had been outvoted to act? Consensus also offers some protection to smaller and poorer nations that might otherwise find themselves overruled by the most powerful countries.
Meanwhile, the failure to agree a summit declaration does not mean climate action stops. Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles are becoming increasingly competitive, while the upheaval in global oil and gas supplies is giving countries another reason to generate their own electricity rather than depend on imported fossil fuels.
The energy transition is moving forward, whatever happens in the UN negotiating rooms. The problem is that it is not moving nearly fast enough for the climate.
Perhaps the most poignant aspect of the failed Antalya Pact is what the countries had apparently been prepared to accept.
The final draft expressed "deep concern" that global warming was expected to exceed 1.5°C in the next few years. It warned that further warming would cause increasingly serious damage, some of it irreversible, and called for urgent action to limit how far temperatures rose above that threshold.
This remarkably strong language had survived into the final version, apparently without provoking the opposition that sank the agreement. Even countries bitterly divided over fossil fuels and finance seemed prepared to acknowledge the scale of the danger.
Yet they couldn't agree on how to respond.
And that, perhaps, is what Antalya tells us about the state of international climate co-operation. The problem isn't simply finding the right words or changing the voting rules. It is persuading countries with very different interests to take action that no international authority can compel them to take.
That was always going to be difficult. In today's divided world, it looks harder than ever.

articles.title_orig: Israeli Political Leaders Denounce ‘Jewish Terrorism’ After West Bank Attacks
articles.title_zh: Israeli Political Leaders Denounce ‘Jewish Terrorism’ After West Bank Attacks
articles.content_orig:
Israeli settlers have attacked several Palestinian towns and villages in the central occupied West Bank, burning cars and damaging property.
The attacks early on Sunday included the burning of 12 vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on the walls of homes in Ramallah and el-Bireh provinces, reported the Palestinian news agency Wafa. The incidents were reported in Kafr Malik village, Deir Abu Mash’al village, and Deir al-Sudan village.
“Residents were awakened around two in the morning by sounds of fire and explosions. They realised the settlers had set fire to cars,” reported Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Odeh from Kafr Malik.
Israeli settler violence has surged across the occupied West Bank since Israel launched its genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza. At least 1,222 people, including 255 children, have been killed in attacks there since Israel launched its war in October 2023 in response to the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.
The Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said there was a significant increase in the number of attacks throughout the Palestinian territory last month.
According to the Palestinian Authority body, there were 3,133 attacks in October, with Israeli forces responsible for 1,764 of them and Israeli settlers 1,369.
The commission said the total number of attacks increased by 53 percent compared with September when 2,051 attacks were recorded. Settler attacks alone rose from 647 in September to 1,369 in October – a 112 percent increase.
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar Party, who has been tasked with forming a new government after Israel’s general election last month, criticised the latest attacks on Sunday.
He wrote on social media that the attacks were “Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word, and it must be called what it is”.
“Sabotage by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermines regional stability, endangers lives and severely damages the national security of the state of Israel and its foreign relations,” he posted on X.
“The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy,” he added, referring to far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
Ben-Gvir rejected the allegations and said Eisenkot was rushing to conclusions. He wrote on social media that Eisenkot’s stance represents a “down payment” to Arab Knesset member Ahmad Tibi in preparation for forming a government with the support of Arab parties.
Settlers are often “escorted by Israeli squads and they do nothing to stop the attackers,” Shai Parnes of the Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem told Al Jazeera.
The Israeli military said it was sending police officers and investigators from the Criminal Identification Unit to the attacked areas “to collect evidence as part of the ongoing investigation”, the military wrote on social media.

articles.title_orig: Amazon snaps up Decart's AI optimization tech for $7.5B as it prepares to sell Trainium chips
articles.title_zh: Amazon snaps up Decart's AI optimization tech for $7.5B as it prepares to sell Trainium chips
articles.content_orig:
Amazon has agreed to acquire a good chunk of Israeli startup Decart.
The e-commerce and cloud giant is paying $7.5 billion for the startup, according to Bloomberg.
Decart has made a name for itself building interactive real-time world models — most recently Oasis 3 — and AI video-generation tools. But under the hood, the company stands out for its Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), software that helps AI models run efficiently on Nvidia, Amazon, and Google’s hardware.
As part of the deal, Amazon will acquire the technology behind DOS, as well as Decart’s founding team and team of AI researchers and engineers, Amazon said in a blog post .
“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, quantum computing, at Amazon. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.”
Amazon, which has so far been using its Trainium chips at its own data centers, is preparing to start selling them to customers as a competitor to Nvidia. Decart’s technology could make it easier for customers to run their workloads on Amazon chips, rather than Nvidia’s, which has been the gold standard so far.
Decart and Amazon did not immediately return requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
articles.title_zh: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
articles.content_orig:
Israel’s military assault on Gaza has caused severe environmental contamination, with signs of toxic pollution found across the entire territory, according to a report published by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS).
The report, published Monday, said the extensive use of explosive and incendiary weapons, airstrikes and fires has made the air, soil and water too dangerous to live in for decades to come.
The scale and intensity of Israel’s bombardment have affected around 78% of Gaza’s landmass, with more than 99% of the territory experiencing potential contamination, the report found.
“The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival,” Oxfam International Executive Director Amitabh Behar said. “This would breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law.”
The report’s authors said that environmental destruction on such a large scale “may constitute, facilitate or provide powerful evidence of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.”
Behar said Palestinians are being exposed to toxins through air, food, water and through direct contact with contaminated soils and debris – risks that will persist unless “recovery actions are prioritized.”
Israel’s foreign ministry called the report “shameful and scandalous” and said Oxfam had “traded its credibility for campaigning.”
“The scale of destruction in Gaza reflects the scale of the terror network Hamas built there, including a 500+ kilometer tunnel system and weapons depots, inside and beneath civilian areas,” the ministry said in a statement to CNN.
The Board of Peace, created by the Trump administration and backed by a UN Security Council resolution, was supposed to oversee implementation of a ceasefire signed between Israel and Hamas more than a year ago, as well as reconstruction of the enclave. Amid a stalled ceasefire plan, the board is widely seen as having failed in that effort and as ineffective at pressuring Israel to meet its commitments.
Israel has refused to allow in heavy equipment needed for large-scale cleanup and rubble removal efforts, saying Hamas could use it for military purposes. The Israeli military office in charge of coordinating aid into Gaza has said that reconstruction will only begin “after Hamas fully disarms.”
Last December, Israel barred dozens of aid organizations, including Oxfam, from working in Gaza, alleging that they failed to comply with new registration restrictions. For the study published on Monday, Oxfam and CEOBS examined satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis, and other open-source data and concluded that contamination is widespread, with serious implications for civilian survival.
But the report cautioned that restrictions on bringing testing equipment and technical expertise into Gaza “continue to prevent a full assessment of the scale and extent of contamination.”
The United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) estimated last year that Israel’s military offensive has generated more than 61 million tons of debris – about as much as 15 Great Pyramids of Giza – which could contain potentially hazardous materials.
Palestinians in Gaza face growing respiratory health risks from dust and pollution from destroyed buildings, as well as a high risk of drinking contaminated water, as water supply systems have been devastated.
Around 85% of Gaza’s water infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed, according to the report, leaving people with roughly just 18 liters of water per person per day for all uses.
The report warns that because Gaza’s health and monitoring systems have been destroyed, much of the harm caused by the toxic waste will go “undetected and unattributed for years.”
Oxfam called on Israel to allow unrestricted access for aid and an environmental assessment.
“Recovery and reconstruction of Gaza must be owned and led by Palestinians themselves,” the organization stated. “It must be rights-based, reparations-oriented, and rooted in accountability. International funding does not replace Israel’s obligation to make reparations for the harm caused by its unlawful acts.”
Israel’s offensive in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023, with estimates of thousands more missing under the rubble. An independent UN Commission of Inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and continues to do so after the US-brokered ceasefire. The Israeli government has forcefully rejected that assessment.

articles.title_orig: Stock Traders Brace for More Volatility After Tech-Driven Rout
articles.title_zh: Stock Traders Brace for More Volatility After Tech-Driven Rout
articles.content_orig:
If you blink, you may have missed it.
Nvidia shares gapped higher at the open by more than 30%, on pace for its biggest one-day gain in 23 years on Monday, following the news just before the bell that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is going to be reinstated.
Investors and traders said that while this reflex rally may have more to run, cautiousness is warranted on Nvidia and the AI trade because of the overhang of investigations into the alleged Chinese espionage involving the company and others, as well as the possibility for data center moratoriums as Democrats take control of Congress and key governor posts in January.
"Am I as bullish on Nvidia now as I was on Friday? Of course not, you can't be," said Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, which counted Nvidia as its largest position as he bought on the dip over the last few weeks. "I'm trimming back."
"All the same issues that were here before Jensen resigned are still here," he added.
The day before Huang resigned on Nov. 12 as CEO, Nvidia closed at $173.73. It's intraday high on Monday was $171.50, up from its recent low around $125 as it was selling off in the wake controversies. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF closed at $506.96 the day before his resignation. It reached a high of $469.35 before losing steam as trading wore on Monday.
Mike Khouw, YieldMax strategist at Tidal Financial Group, told CNBC on Monday that there were "sighs of relief," "applause" and even "cheering" among investors at the news of Huang's potential reinstatement. But he also said there are still considerable risks facing the AI trade.
Jensen Huang was not the only problem at Nvidia, he said, and there are still many vulnerabilities in the overall AI trade, which should give investors pause. Credit-sensitive companies are still at risk of faltering, Khouw added.
The national security implications of the scandal that has rocked Nvidia and the global AI trade more broadly aren't going away any time soon even as the Trump administration assured the Nvidia board there were none . Investors on Wall Street are expressing strategic concerns about ways to play the tech space just as lawmakers in Washington are demanding answers.
Democrats are demanding answers on what exactly happened with Nvidia and the Chinese government.
"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a Monday statement. "The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement."
House Ways and Means ranking member Richard Neal (D-Mass.) stressed the importance of Congressional oversight in determining the best course of action to move forward. The outcome of any Congressional investigations will likely be crucial for Nvidia's long-term viability as an investment opportunity, especially since the company does so much international business.
"This is an export control issue," Neal told CNBC on Monday. "Congress is not subservient to this president or any other president as it relates to trade and tariff policies. This is a trade related issue."
Many of the same Democrats will call for a slowdown in the data center buildout, a strong issue for the public partly responsible for their Blue Wave earlier this month.
"You're going to have to work your way through what these data center moratoriums all mean," said Niles. "Now I think the broader market keeps going but I am not as convinced on the move in the data-center centric names from here."
To be sure, many Wall Street analysts were rushing to upgrade Nvidia's stock on Monday after Huang's reinstatement. Most restored price targets well above $200 with one as high as $270. But many traders think the rebound may fail before getting back to those levels.
Famed short seller Michael Burry, who made a boatload betting against Nvidia with put options as it cratered, told his Substack audience that he thinks the rebound here could be "outsized," especially with low volume in the market overall because of the Thanksgiving holiday this week.
But he too sees the rally eventually losing steam.
"Jensen being back without much more information might even restore NVDA to the high 100s," Burry wrote. "I won't short it on this information I have today until it gets closer to or maybe hurdles $200."

Now Bar live notifications
Samsung is moving its Now Bar live notifications closer to Apple's Dynamic Island, with changes to both their position and the way you switch between ongoing activities. We've tested the new layout in early Galaxy S27 series software.
Samsung is working on a new look for the Now Bar's live notifications, and the resemblance to Apple's Dynamic Island is hard to miss. We've exclusively discovered the changes in early Galaxy S27 series software, offering a glimpse of how Samsung could present ongoing activities in a future update.
On current versions of One UI, the live notification pill sits beside the clock on the left. Samsung's new layout moves it to the top center, in the area around the front camera.
The timer countdown, Torch indicator, and expandable activity controls you see here are familiar features already in One UI. The new layout displays those existing updates from this central position.
Centered torch Now Bar pill
Centered timer Now Bar pill
Samsung is also changing how you switch between compact live notification pills. Currently, you swipe up and down to move between ongoing activities. In the version we tested, you swipe left and right instead, without first expanding the pill.
That sideways switching gesture, combined with the placement around the selfie camera, gives Samsung's existing live notifications a more Dynamic Island-like feel.
Now Bar settings also include a Moment effects page, with Sports as the only listed download. It offers celebrations for your favorite teams' scores and wins in selected sports supported by Google Sports.
Samsung has already introduced sports animations in the One UI 9.5 beta . The broader Moment effects name could leave room for other types of effects later, but additional categories haven't been confirmed.
All of these changes are still under development and could be revised before Samsung brings them to Galaxy devices. They will likely debut with the Galaxy S27 series before reaching existing devices through the One UI 9.5 update .

articles.title_orig: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
articles.title_zh: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday lauded an "exemplary" military operation that sank one of Russia's newest ships at a Libyan port, after Kyiv's forces struck their target with several domestically made naval drones.
The incident followed a suspected Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea on Saturday and occurred less than a week after damage was inflicted on Russian President Vladimir Putin 's prized Crimea bridge.
In a social media post , Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces deployed seven sea drones to attack the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, at Benghazi's port in the early hours of Sunday morning. Ukraine's president posted dramatic video footage showing Ukraine's naval drones triggering a massive explosion on the Russian ship.
"Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk. It's one of their newest ships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale war," Zelenskyy said. "We continue our operations in designated waters," he added.
Satellite imagery taken on Sunday showed the Merkury mostly underwater, having capsized
The Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons, was hit by Ukrainian forces. A Ka-27 military helicopter on the Merkury was also destroyed.
Asked about reports of attacks on Russian ships off the coast of Libya, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said information on this would be provided via the Defense Ministry.
The Security Service of Ukraine, the SBU, said Monday that the attacks "once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics have no safe routes even far beyond the Black Sea," according to a Google translation.
"Such unique special operations destroy the enemy's logistical capabilities and force Russia to pay for aggression even at a strategic distance from Ukraine," the SBU said via Telegram.
The United Nations Support Mission in Libya, or UNSMIL, expressed "serious concern" over the drone attacks in a statement saying the country "cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts."
"UNSMIL calls for an immediate, independent and transparent investigation to establish the facts and hold those responsible to account," it added.
The incident is not the first time Libya has seen attacks linked to the Russia-Ukraine war near its territory.
In March, Moscow's Transport Ministry accused Ukraine of striking the Arctic Metagaz, a liquefied natural gas tanker, as part of a suspected sea drone attack in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta.

articles.title_orig: There’s a Terrible, Unexpected Consequence of Rome’s New Trevi Fountain Rules
articles.title_zh: There’s a Terrible, Unexpected Consequence of Rome’s New Trevi Fountain Rules
articles.content_orig:
T he €2 ($2.28) entry fee introduced at Rome's Trevi Fountain may be weighing on the centuries-old tradition of tossing coins into the water.
Coin donations from the landmark in the Italian capital fell by about $228,000 in the first nine months of the year compared with the same period last year, The Guardian reported.
Caritas, a charity linked to the Catholic Church in Rome, collects the coins and uses them to fund food banks and other social assistance projects. Giustino Trincia, Caritas Rome director, said restricting direct access to the fountain's basin area may have contributed to the decline. The coins have generated about $1.71 million a year for the charity.
Under the system that took effect in February, only Rome residents and visitors who pay the $2.28 fee can reach the basin area during daytime hours.
The measure aims to ease overcrowding at the historic structure and raise revenue for maintenance work. The fountain is an 18th-century Baroque monument that marks the endpoint of an ancient aqueduct.
The Rome municipality collected about $496,000 in entrance fees during the system's first month. Officials plan to use the revenue to keep crowds under control at the fountain, which 4.4 million tourists visited in 2025, and to finance maintenance of the fountain and other historic structures in the city.
Jeff Clinton, a tourist from the United States, said he found a 1-cent coin on a Rome street and wanted to toss it into the fountain but changed his mind because access to the basin area requires payment. Eric and Patty, a couple from New York, said they had no coins with them and did not want to pay the fee to get closer.
Alan and Ying, a couple from Australia, paid the fee but did not throw a coin. They said they saw no other tourists continuing the tradition around them and decided not to take part.
A Caritas Rome spokesperson said this year's collection figures do not yet include foreign currencies, meaning the actual decline may be smaller than it appears.
The tradition of tossing coins into the Trevi Fountain is thought to date back to ancient pagan rituals in which people made offerings to water gods. The practice spread worldwide largely through the 1954 romantic comedy "Three Coins in the Fountain."
According to popular legend, a coin tossed into the fountain guarantees a return to Rome.

articles.title_orig: AI rally set to add $2 trillion to Nasdaq-100 as Huang returns to Nvidia helm
articles.title_zh: AI rally set to add $2 trillion to Nasdaq-100 as Huang returns to Nvidia helm
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street spent last week dumping anything tied to AI. It's spending Monday buying it back.
The Invesco QQQ Trust ( QQQ ), the fund that tracks the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 ( ^NDX ), opened almost 8% higher, its biggest jump at the open since it launched in 1999. Its closest rivals for largest jumps came in 2000 and 2001 as the dot-com bubble was bursting and big rallies had a habit of fizzling.
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ) opened 5% higher. Among Mondays since 1993, only Oct. 13, 2008, in the depths of the financial crisis, started with a bigger jump.
The rally is holding. By midday, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) is up more than 4% and on track for its best day since April 2025, the Nasdaq-100 is up more than 6%, and the CBOE Volatility Index ( ^VIX ) is down about 8 points.
The surge comes as Nvidia ( NVDA ) brought back Jensen Huang as CEO and after the S&P 500 slid into a correction last week.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) opened 15% higher, its biggest jump at the open since it launched in 2001 and well past its previous record of about 9% in October 2002.
Nvidia opened up 33% on Huang's return and is on track for one of the best days in the company's history, which tops out at a 42% gain in March 2000. Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ), Micron ( MU ), and AMD ( AMD ) opened roughly 12% to 21% higher.
Read more: Buy Nvidia stock or wait? A guide to making the call on any stock.
Not everyone thinks the panic has run its course. Options sentiment "screams" the worst levels since the pandemic and Liberation Day, Roundhill Investments chief investment strategist Drew Pettit told Yahoo Finance, "but it's not a washout."
History sides with the bulls, eventually. In the 20 times since 1993 that SPY opened Monday 2% or more higher, it was higher a year later in 17 of those, with a median gain of about 25%, roughly double that of a typical year, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Creative Planning's Charlie Bilello found a similar pattern . Last week's nearly 9% drop was the S&P 500's 12th-worst week since 1950, he noted, and after the worst weeks, stocks averaged a 26% gain over the next year, compared with 11% otherwise.
Evercore ISI's Julian Emanuel is in that camp too, writing over the weekend, "Bull Market intact as double-digit EPS gains likely ahead."
In half of those 20 cases, SPY slipped back below the prior Friday's low within three months, most often within two weeks. Think of it as the morning after a big night out. The headache usually comes back before it goes away.
Even so, eight of those 10 were higher a year later. The two closest matches to this setup, October 2008 and May 2010, each paired a brutal week with a big Monday open, sank further over the next three months and were about 15% higher a year later.
That puts Friday's low, about 6,883 on the S&P 500, in focus. And the Fed isn't riding to the rescue , with Wall Street still pricing a December rate hike and every correction that hits with inflation speeding up this fast turning into a bear market .
BTIG's strategists aren't calling a bottom yet. "We don't think this is the final low, but we are looking for a short-term rally back towards 7250-7350 before likely turning lower again," they wrote over the weekend.
As of midday Monday, the S&P 500 is already knocking on the bottom of that range.

articles.content_orig:
Update [ Mon 23rd Nov 2026, 2:50pm ]: Well, the patch notes are out! Rockstar Games mentions seven official fixes for the update, and none of them are specifically to do with the Xbox Series S or other things like how bright the game is.
Nevertheless, there's always a chance they've made some extra tweaks under the hood.
Here are the official seven fixes in GTA 6's first post-launch update (November 23):
Original Story: GTA 6 only officially launched late last week, but Rockstar Games has already pushed out a new update (01.002.002) for the game across Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S (along with PS5), rolling out as of a few hours ago.
You're looking at a download size of around 1.6GB for update 1.0.2 on Xbox Series X and S.
In terms of what's included, Rockstar has yet to issue any official patch notes, and we'll have to wait and see whether anything is distributed. We'll obviously update this article with the patch notes if they're made available to us.
Players are trying to make their own discoveries in the meantime, with suggestions that the game may run smoother on Xbox Series S now, that saving your game returns you to the exact same spot instead of your safehouse (although this seemed to be happening for us already), and that the first-person glitch is still working as things stand.
All of these could be akin to placebo effects though, so take them with a pinch of salt:
As you can see from one of the impressions above, there's a suggestion that the game seems brighter now, which perhaps could have something to do with the borked HDR calibration tool that we discussed the other day .
That said, who knows whether these are areas that have actually been targeted for the update, or whether they're just happy coincidences that some players are experiencing. In any case, we'll keep an eye out for any official confirmations.

articles.title_orig: More Americans pay this Obama-era investment tax every year — how to avoid it
articles.title_zh: More Americans pay this Obama-era investment tax every year — how to avoid it
articles.content_orig:
Every year, more Americans pay an extra tax levy on their investment gains — but there's still time to reduce or avoid that bill for 2026, experts say.
Net investment income tax , or NIIT, is a 3.8% levy on investment income once earnings exceed $200,000 for single filers or $250,000 for married couples filing jointly. The tax was enacted in 2010 under President Barack Obama to help fund healthcare via the Affordable Care Act .
Unlike the federal income tax or capital gains brackets , the NIIT earnings limits don't adjust annually for inflation.
As a result, "more clients get hit every year," said certified financial planner Michael Walstedt, founding advisor of Reliant Wealth Advisory in Hoboken, New Jersey.
Roughly 5.6% of tax returns included NIIT for 2025, according to IRS data released in November for returns processed through mid-July 2026. That's up from about 3.7% for the same time frame in 2021.
As more investors pay NIIT, here are some key things to know.
NIIT applies when you have investment income and your earnings exceed the modified adjusted gross income, or MAGI, limits, according to certified financial planner Marianela Collado , CEO of Tobias Financial Advisors in Plantation, Florida.
"The trick is to keep an eye on both of these numbers," said Collado, who is also a certified public accountant and member of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council .
For the NIIT earnings limit, MAGI is typically the same as adjusted gross income , or AGI. One exception would be if you have foreign income, which changes the calculation. You can find last year's AGI on line 11a of your 2025 tax return .
MAGI limits by filing status
Married filing jointly: $250,000
Married filing separately: $125,000
Head of household (with qualifying person): $200,000
Qualifying widow(er) with dependent child: $250,000
NIIT applies to investment income, which includes interest, dividends, annuities, royalties, certain rents, and more. It can also include capital gains from a primary home sale , for profits that exceed the IRS exclusions. The exclusion is $250,000 for single filers or $500,000 for married couples.
The levy stacks on top of regular income tax rates, or capital gains tax — which can be 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on earnings. That means higher earners can pay up to 23.8% on investment income, including long-term capital gains and NIIT.
The NIIT calculation is 3.8% multiplied by the lesser of:
For example, if your MAGI is $30,000 above the NIIT earnings limit and you have $100,000 of investment income, you would pay 3.8% of $30,000, or $1,140.
Alternatively, if your MAGI is $120,000 above the threshold and you have $100,000 of investment income, you would owe 3.8% of $100,000, or $3,800.
As year-end approaches, investors should run projections to estimate their adjusted gross income, which can impact NIIT, among other tax consequences, experts say.
If you're above the NIIT limits, you could reduce AGI by boosting pretax 401(k) deferrals or health savings account contributions, according to Collado with Tobias Financial Advisors.
While employee 401(k) deferrals must happen by Dec. 31, you have until next year's tax deadline for health savings account contributions for 2026.
You might also try to avoid selling assets before year-end, which could further boost AGI, experts say. Of course, any current-year tax moves should consider your long-term financial goals.
Amid recent stock market volatility , investors may also consider so-called tax-loss harvesting , which uses losses to offset other portfolio gains, Walstedt with Reliant Wealth Advisory said.
If your losses exceed profits, you can subtract up to $3,000 from regular income. After that, you can carry remaining losses into future tax years.
However, if you're planning to reinvest the sale proceeds, you need to know the " wash sale rule ," which blocks the tax-loss harvesting tax break for buying a "substantially identical" asset within 30 days before or after the sale.

Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas has extended his contract with the ⁠chip designer to lead the company through 2033, confirming his ​leadership role ​at the ​firm amid speculation that Nvidia could tap him for the top job after Jensen Huang's resignation.
Nvidia's board ⁠had ‌approached Haas in its search ⁠for a successor to Huang, the Financial Times reported earlier this month, following Huang's exit amid revelations of extramarital affairs ‌including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Analysts had also pointed to Haas ​as a solid candidate for the CEO role at Nvidia, given he spent his formative years at the company, rising to ⁠vice president and general manager of its computing products ‌business, before joining Arm in ‌2013.
Haas became the British chipmaker's chief executive in 2022 and oversaw its return to public markets ⁠through a $65 billion Nasdaq listing the following year.
Arm licenses ⁠processor designs used across smartphones, ⁠PCs, servers and connected devices.
"I've never been more confident about Arm's future... I'm wholly ​committed to realizing ‌Arm's full potential for many years to come," Haas said in a statement on Monday.
Haas will also assume the role of vice chairman of ​SoftBank Group , effective December 1, Arm ‌Holdings said on Monday.
